title: Foundational links into polynomial, rational, radical, exponential, and sequence concepts
status: AI-assisted desk review; educator confirmation pending
method_note: Draft classifications reason from the current concept-cluster outcomes. They are not independent expert sign-off or empirical validation. The proposed checks have not been run yet.

EDGE-057: The polynomial cluster uses powers of the variable and interprets degree/coefficient structure; exponent meaning is part of reading polynomial terms, though a brief exponent refresher can be embedded in the first polynomial lesson.
Ask learners to read and compare x, x², and 3x² + 2x; check whether they can explain the exponent/degree meaning and carry out products without an exponent-law prerequisite gap.
EDGE-059: Integer factors and common multiples can support factor intuition, but polynomial factorization is not simply prime factorization. Treat FND-007 as a source of examples, not a gate to learning algebraic identities.

Test factoring simple polynomials such as x² + 5x + 6 and x² - 9 after teaching polynomial structure; compare performance with a separate numerical-factor diagnostic to see what actually blocks progress.
EDGE-065: Rational expressions are quotients of expressions/polynomials and can be introduced without prior fluency with powers and integer exponents. Powers are useful for later rational-expression examples but not for the basic fraction/domain idea.
Assess simplification and excluded-value reasoning on (x² - 1)/(x - 1) and simple linear quotients before using exponent-heavy examples; insert an exponent refresher only when required.
EDGE-066: The radicals/rational-exponents cluster directly relies on the meaning of powers and exponent notation. Real-domain rules and equivalence manipulations build on that base.
Use conversion tasks between square roots and fractional exponents, simplify simple powers, then solve a radical equation and check the result. Distinguish exponent meaning errors from domain errors.
EDGE-068: For the full radicals/rational-exponents outcome, learners need to reason about real-number domains, intervals, and valid values—especially even roots and constraints introduced by transformations. Teach any missing subskill locally as a bridge.

Give real-domain tasks such as √(x - 2), distinguish domain from output range, and ask which values make a proposed equation meaningful; identify whether interval/number-order reasoning is a genuine blocker.
EDGE-070: Integer-exponent meaning underpins exponential functions as repeated multiplicative change and supports the inverse relationship between exponentials and logarithms.
Translate repeated percentage growth into an exponential rule, compare it with a linear sequence, and explain the role of the exponent; check this before teaching logarithms as the inverse operation.
EDGE-072: Real-number order and interval notation help state domains/ranges and logarithm constraints, but the essential positive-input restriction for logarithms can be taught explicitly in ALG-017. The whole FND-016 cluster is broader than the minimum needed.

Teach log input restrictions locally, then test domain/range statements and interval notation separately. If learners understand positive inputs but struggle only with notation, treat FND-016 as a repair path rather than a hard gate.
EDGE-074: Sequences and patterns can be introduced through finite lists, tables, and recursive rules before exponent fluency. Powers are useful for geometric sequences and exponential patterns but not for every sequence.
Assess arithmetic and recursive sequence rules without exponents first, then geometric sequences with powers. Separate the objectives and only require FND-014 for the latter.
